rows.speaker: محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet is quoted as saying that judges decide by outward evidence while God knows inner realities.
rows.anchor: نحن نحكم بالظاهر والله يتولى السرائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three incidents apply one rule: bear the lesser harm to prevent the greater harm.
rows.anchor: عند تعارض الضررين يجب تحمل الأدنى لدفع الأعلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses judged by outwardly known law, while the unnamed sage knew inward realities; in this knowledge the sage surpassed Moses.
rows.anchor: مرتبة موسى عليه السلام في معرفة الشرائع والأحكام بناء الأمر على الظواهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boy's continued life would harm his parents' faith and worldly life; revelation showed the harm from killing him was lesser.
rows.anchor: بقاء ذلك الغلام حيا كان مفسدة للوالدين في دينهم وفي دنياهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Building the wall imposed a lesser hardship than its collapse, which would destroy the orphans' property.
rows.anchor: المشقة الحاصلة بسبب الإقدام على إقامة ذلك الجدار ضررها أقل من سقوطه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sage knew inward realities and based true rulings on them, whereas Moses' rulings followed outward appearances.
rows.anchor: كان مخصوصا بالوقوف على بواطن الأشياء وبالأطلاع على حقائقها كما هي عليها في أنفسها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Moses could not learn the sage's inward knowledge as ordinary instruction, the encounter taught him that spiritual knowledge completes legal knowledge and comes through purification of the heart.
rows.anchor: وأما العلم ببواطن الأشياء فإنما يمكن تحصيله بناء على تصفية الباطن وتجريد النفس

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī infers that a poor person is needier than a miskin because these boat-owning people are called miskin.
rows.anchor: احتج بهذه الآية على أن حال الفقير في الضر والحاجة أشد من حال المسكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sage damaged the boat to keep the tyrant from seizing it; the aim was not to drown its passengers, and partial damage was the lesser loss.
rows.anchor: ما كان مقصودي من تخريق تلك السفينة تغريق أهلها بل مقصودي أن ذلك الملك الظالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether an outsider may damage another's property for this purpose depends on the law; a comparable partial payment to a highway robber can preserve the rest and benefit the owner.
rows.anchor: هذا مما يختلف أحواله بحسب اختلاف الشرائع فلعل هذا المعنى كان جائزا في تلك الشريعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The damage had to leave the boat usable, since destroying it would not be a lesser loss than seizure.
rows.anchor: أن ذلك التخريق وجب أن يكون واقعا على وجه لا تبطل به تلك السفينة بالكلية

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reads warāʾahum as ahead of them, since what is absent from view can be called behind or in front.
rows.anchor: هكذا قاله الفراء وتفسيره قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading places the king behind the place from which the boat's owner embarked or would return.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون الملك كان من وراء الموضع الذي يركب منه صاحبه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One report says the boy was an adult highway robber whose parents defended and excused his wrongdoing, risking their own sin and perhaps disbelief.
rows.anchor: قيل : إن ذلك الغلام كان بالغا وكان يقطع الطريق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another report says the boy was still a child, but God knew he would commit those harms as an adult.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه كان صبيا إلا أن الله تعالى علم منه أنه لو صار بالغا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here khashiya means fear or a strong presumption; the sage's action was licensed by God's knowledge and revelation.
rows.anchor: الخشية بمعنى الخوف وغلبة الظن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of yurhiqahumā is that the boy would drive his parents toward transgression by making them defend or follow his evil acts.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد أن ذلك الغلام يحمل أبويه على الطغيان والكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading is that the boy himself treated his parents with the conduct of tyrants and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المعنى أن ذلك الولد كان يعاشرهما معاشرة الطغاة الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Killing on the basis of such a suspicion is permissible only when revelation confirms it.
rows.anchor: إذا تأكد ذلك الظن بوحي الله جاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakāh means religious purity and righteousness; the replacement child would be better in faith and more affectionate toward the parents.
rows.anchor: أي دينا وصلاحا ، وقيل : إن ذكره الزكاة ههنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sage's mention of purity answers Moses' objection about killing an innocent soul: the boy was pure then, but God knew he would later become rebellious; an adult reading takes purity as no visible offense.
rows.anchor: إن تلك النفس وإن كانت زاكية طاهرة في الحال إلا أنه تعالى علم منها أنها إذا بلغت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aqrabu ruḥman means the replacement would show greater compassion and dutiful affection to the parents.
rows.anchor: أي يكون هذا البدل أقرب عطفا ورحمة بأبويه

rows.speaker: رُوي
rows.claim: An anonymous report says the parents had a daughter who married a prophet and bore a prophet through whom God guided a great community.
rows.anchor: روى أنه ولدت لهما جارية تزوجها نبي فولدت نبيا هدى الله على يديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr read yubaddilahumā with an open bāʾ and doubled dāl; the others use the alternate light form, also found at 66:5 and 68:32.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وأبو عمرو يبدلهما بفتح الباء وتشديد الدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir in one transmission attributed to Abū ʿAmr reads ruḥman with ḥāʾ ḍammah; the others read it with sukūn, both being dialect forms.
rows.anchor: قراءة ابن عامر في إحدى الروايتين عن أبي عمرو رحما بضم الحاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God had the sage shore up the nearly fallen wall to protect the orphans' treasure in view of their rights and their father's righteousness.
rows.anchor: فأراد الله إبقاء ذلك الكنز على ذينك اليتيمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The place called a village earlier is also called a city in the wall explanation.
rows.anchor: سمى ذلك الموضع قرية حيث قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treasure was money: that is the normal meaning of kanz and the command that the boys extract it supports this reading.
rows.anchor: إنه كان مالا وهذا هو الصحيح لوجهين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative says the treasure was knowledge, reasoning that a righteous father's treasure would be learning rather than wealth.
rows.anchor: كان علما بدليل أنه قال

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further report describes a gold tablet inscribed with maxims about trusting providence, provision, death, judgment, and the world's instability.
rows.anchor: وقيل : كان لوحا من ذهب مكتوب فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shows that parents' righteousness brings care for their children; Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad says seven generations separated the boys from their righteous ancestor.
rows.anchor: وعن جعفر بن محمد كان بين الغلامين وبين الأب الصالح سبعة آباء

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: In a dialogue with a Kharijite, al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī says the boys' property was preserved through their father's righteousness; the Kharijite objects that his own forebears were better.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن ابن علي أنه قال لبعض الخوارج

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account says the righteous father held people's deposits and returned them safely.
rows.anchor: وذكروا أيضا أن ذلك الأب الصالح كان الناس يضعون الودائع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boys may have been unaware of the treasure while their absent guardian knew it, explaining how they could later recover it.
rows.anchor: لعل اليتيمين كانا جاهلين به إلا أن وصيهما كان عالما به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sage acted by God's command rather than personal judgment, since damaging property and spilling blood require decisive revelation.
rows.anchor: ما فعلت ما رأيت من هذه الأحوال عن أمري واجتهادي ورأيي وإنما فعلته بأمر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The changes from I wanted, to we wanted, to your Lord willed assign the boat's damage to the sage, the grave killing to a majestic plural, and care for the orphans to God.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر رعاية مصالح اليتيمين لأجل صلاح أبيهما أضافه إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about Dhū al-Qarnayn belongs to the questions Jews told the polytheists to ask Muhammad, alongside the Sleepers and the Spirit.
rows.anchor: أن اليهود أمروا المشركين أن يسألوا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The first identity proposed is Alexander son of Philip: the Qur'an places his realm at the far west, east, and north, a scale matching the historically famous Alexander.
rows.anchor: أنه هو الاسكندر بن فيلبوس اليوناني قالوا والدليل عليه أن القرآن دل على أن الرجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account recounts Alexander's conquests across the Mediterranean, Egypt, Syria, Armenia, Persia, India, and China, followed by his death at Shahrazur.
rows.anchor: ثم توجه نحو دارا بن دارا وهزمه مرات إلى أن قتله صاحب حرسه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation of Alexander's epithet says he reached the sun's two horns, its rising and setting places, like Ardashir's epithet for long arms.
rows.anchor: أنه لقب بهذا اللقب لأجل بلوغه قرني الشمس

rows.speaker: الفرس
rows.claim: The Persians claimed Alexander was Darius the Great's son by Philip's daughter, who had returned to Philip while pregnant; Razi calls this a lie and says Alexander addressed Darius as father out of humility and honor.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي قاله الفرس إنما ذكروه لأنهم أرادوا أن يجعلوه من نسل ملوك العجم

rows.speaker: أبو الريحان الهروي
rows.claim: Al-Bīrūnī transmits a second identity: the Himyarite Abu Karib Shammar ibn Abir ibn Afriqish, said to have ruled the earth's east and west.
rows.anchor: إن ذا القرنين هو أبو كرب شمر بن عبير

rows.speaker: شاعر من حمير
rows.claim: A Himyarite poet praises Dhū al-Qarnayn as a Muslim king who reached east and west seeking dominion from a noble lord.
rows.anchor: قد كان ذو القرنين قبلي مسلما

rows.speaker: أبو الريحان
rows.claim: Al-Bīrūnī considers the Himyarite identification more plausible because Yemenite rulers commonly bore names beginning with Dhū.
rows.anchor: ويشبه أن يكون هذا القول أقرب لأن الأذواء كانوا من اليمن

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A third view identifies Dhū al-Qarnayn as an unnamed righteous servant whom God made ruler over the earth and endowed with knowledge and wisdom.
rows.anchor: أنه كان عبدا صالحا ملكه الله الأرض وأعطاه العلم والحكمة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Asked by Ibn al-Kawwāʾ whether he was king or prophet, ʿAlī says he was neither but a righteous servant, struck on one horn in God's obedience, revived, struck on the other, revived again, and then received kingship.
rows.anchor: عن ذي القرنين وقال أملك هو أم نبي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says two generations of people died during his lifetime.
rows.anchor: سمي بذي القرنين لأنه انقرض في وقته قرنان من الناس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation says the two sides of his head were copper.
rows.anchor: قيل كان صفحتا رأسه من نحاس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another says he wore something resembling two horns on his head.
rows.anchor: كان على رأسه ما يشبه القرنين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further explanation says his crown had two horns.
rows.anchor: الخامس : ( كان ) لتاجه قرنان

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says he was called Dhū al-Qarnayn because he traversed the earth's two horns, its east and west.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سمي ذا القرنين لأنه طاف قرني الدنيا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says he had two braids.
rows.anchor: كان له قرنان أي ضفيرتان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another says light guided him ahead while darkness followed behind when God subjected both to him.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى سخر له النور والظلمة فإذا سرى يهديه النور من أمامه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: He may have been named for bravery, like a ram that butts its peers.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يلقب بذلك لشجاعته كما يسمى الشجاع كبشا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A dream in which he climbed the heavens and grasped the sun's two horns and sides supposedly gave him the name.
rows.anchor: رأى في المنام كأنه صعد الفلك فتعلق بطرفي الشمس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One last explanation says he entered both light and darkness.
rows.anchor: سمي بذلك لأنه دخل النور والظلمة

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: A fourth identity says Dhū al-Qarnayn was an angel; ʿUmar rebukes someone for using an angel's name when people already bear prophets' names.
rows.anchor: عن عمر أنه سمع رجلا يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi favors Alexander because an empire spanning the inhabited world would be famous, and Alexander is the ruler known to history for such dominion.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول أظهر لأجل الدليل الذي ذكرناه وهو أن مثل هذا الملك العظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He flags a serious objection to identifying him as Alexander: Alexander followed Aristotle, so honoring him would seem to validate Aristotle's doctrine, which Razi says cannot be accepted.
rows.anchor: كان تلميذ أرسططاليس الحكيم وكان على مذهبه فتعظيم الله إياه يوجب الحكم بأن مذهب أرسططاليس حق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some argue Dhū al-Qarnayn was a prophet: God's full empowerment in religion points to prophethood, the general gift includes a means to prophethood, and direct divine speech implies prophethood.
rows.anchor: منهم من قال : إنه كان نبيا واحتجوا عليه بوجوه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Others say he was a righteous servant but not a prophet.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال إنه كان عبدا صالحا وما كان نبيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future tense in sa-atlū means the recitation will occur if God enables it, reveals it, and informs the Prophet of its details.
rows.anchor: معناه إني سأفعل هذا إن وفقني الله تعالى عليه وأنزل فيه وحيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamkīn may mean empowerment through prophethood or kingship; Razi prefers prophethood as the higher and more excellent reading.
rows.anchor: والأول أولى لأن التمكين بسبب النبوة أعلى من التمكين بسبب الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabab originally means rope and by extension anything used to reach an aim, including knowledge, power, or equipment.
rows.anchor: السبب في أصل اللغة عبارة عن الحبل ثم استعير لكل ما يتوصل به إلى المقصود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who regard him as a prophet say the granted means included a path to prophethood; those denying it restrict the phrase to what was needed to govern his realm.
rows.anchor: من جملة الأشياء النبوة فهذه الآية تدل على أنه تعالى أعطاه الطريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restricting the general phrase to royal necessities departs from its apparent generality without evidence.
rows.anchor: إن تخصيص العموم خلاف الظاهر فلا يصار إليه إلا بدليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Abū ʿAmr read fattabaʿa with doubled tāʾ, meaning he followed or traveled a route; the others use the light hamzated form.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو فاتبع بتشديد التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He sought to reach the west by following a route that would take him there.
rows.anchor: أراد بلوغ المغرب فأتبع سببا يوصله إليه حتى بلغه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several readers use ḥāmiyah, meaning hot, including Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim; others read ḥamiʾah, muddy, ascribed here to Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي وأبو بكر عن عاصم في عين حامية بالألف من غير همزة

rows.speaker: محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet tells Abū Dharr that the sun sets in a hot spring, supporting the ḥāmiyah reading.
rows.anchor: فإنها تغرب في عين حامية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: At Muʿāwiyah's recitation of ḥāmiyah, Ibn ʿAbbās insists on ḥamiʾah; Ibn ʿUmar follows the caliph, while Kaʿb says the sun sets in water and mud according to the Torah.
rows.anchor: فقرأ معاوية حامية بألف فقال ابن عباس حمئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two readings do not conflict: the same spring can be both hot and muddy.
rows.anchor: لا تنافي بين الحمئة والحامية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun cannot literally enter an earthly spring: the earth is spherical, the heavens surround it, people cannot live near the sun, and the sun is vastly larger than Earth.
rows.anchor: ثبت بالدليل أن الأرض كرة وأن السماء محيطة بها

rows.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
rows.claim: One interpretation says that at the western limit of habitation the sun only appears to sink into a dark hollow, as it appears to sink into the sea to a sailor who cannot see the shore.
rows.anchor: هذا هو التأويل الذي ذكره أبو علي الجبائي في تفسيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation says western lands are surrounded by hot seas containing black mud, so the setting appears to occur in muddy, hot water.
rows.anchor: أن للجانب الغربي من الأرض مساكن يحيط البحر بها

rows.speaker: أهل الأخبار
rows.claim: Storytellers say the sun sets in an actual water-and-mud spring; Razi rejects this because observations of eclipses and differing local times show the sun remains visible elsewhere, and God's speech cannot contradict certainty.
rows.anchor: قال أهل الأخبار : إن الشمس تغيب في عين كثيرة الماء والحمأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ʿindahā may refer to the sun, making nearby residents seem to live by it, or to the spring; on the latter reading the preceding figurative explanation applies.
rows.anchor: الضمير في قوله عندها إلى ماذا يعود ؟ فيه قولان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's direct address to Dhū al-Qarnayn indicates that he was a prophet; interpreting it as speech through other prophets departs from the plain sense.
rows.anchor: يدل على أنه تعالى تكلم معه من غير واسطة

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports an extraordinary city there with twelve thousand gates; without its residents' noise, people would hear the sun's fall.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جريج : هناك مدينة لها إثنا عشر ألف باب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The western people were disbelievers, and God let Dhū al-Qarnayn choose between punishing those persisting in unbelief and pardoning them.
rows.anchor: يدل على أن سكان آخر المغرب كانوا كفارا فخير الله ذا القرنين فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This choice is ijtihād about what best serves them, comparable to the Prophet's choice concerning captives; most commentators say punishment means killing and kindness means leaving them alive.
rows.anchor: هذا التخيير على معنى الإجتهاد في أصلح الأمرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wrongdoer is one who persists in unbelief, as shown by the contrast with the believer; his worldly punishment is death, followed by a terrible punishment from God.
rows.anchor: أي ظلم نفسه بالإقامة على الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ read jazāʾ al-ḥusnā in the accusative and indefinite; the others read it nominative with annexation.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the nominative reading, the phrase can mean reward for good deeds or a reward described as the best recompense; the accusative means the best reward is his as recompense.
rows.anchor: فعلى القراءة الأولى يكون التقدير فله الحسنى جزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhū al-Qarnayn promised easy, not burdensome, commands such as alms and taxation; yusrā is also read with two ḍammas.
rows.anchor: أي لا نأمره بالصعب الشاق ولكن بالسهل الميسر من الزكاة والخراج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the eastern limit of inhabited lands, one view says there were no trees, mountains, or buildings to shade the people, who retreated underground or into water at sunrise and worked after sunset.
rows.anchor: أنه ليس هناك شجر ولا جبل ولا أبنية تمنع من وقوع شعاع الشمس عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view says they had no clothes and remained naked like animals; books of astronomy attribute this to many Zanj and equatorial peoples.
rows.anchor: أن معناه أنه لا ثياب لهم ويكونون كسائر الحيوانات عراة أبدا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A traveler's account describes people beyond China using one ear as bedding and the other as clothing, hearing the sun's sound, then sheltering underground and cooking fish in its heat.
rows.anchor: سافرت حتى جاوزت الصين فسألت عن هؤلاء القوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Thus” may mean God knew Dhū al-Qarnayn was fit to rule as he followed routes to distant lands.
rows.anchor: كذلك فعل ذو القرنين اتبع هذه الأسباب حتى بلغ ما بلغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it refers to the condition of these people as God revealed it, or says their treatment matched that of the western people.
rows.anchor: كذلك جعل الله أمر هؤلاء القوم على ما قد أعلم رسوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A final parsing ends the sentence at kathālika: God found the people as Dhū al-Qarnayn found them, and already knew their circumstances.
rows.anchor: أنه تم الكلام عند قوله كذلك والمعنى أنه تعالى قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After reaching east and west, Dhū al-Qarnayn followed another route to the gap between the barriers, equipped by God with knowledge and power.
rows.anchor: لما بلغ المشرق والمغرب أتبع سببا آخر وسلك الطريق حتى بلغ بين السدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ in the vowels of saddayn/saddan; al-Kisāʾī says the forms are dialect variants, while Abū ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Anbārī distinguish human-made barriers with fatḥah from God's creation with ḍammah.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي : هما لغتان ، وقيل : ما كان

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf explains the ḍamma form as a passive noun for what God made and the fatḥah form as an event people produce.
rows.anchor: السد بالضم فعل بمعنى مفعول أي هو مما فعله الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barrier site is placed in the north, variously between Armenia and Azerbaijan or at the Turkic frontier.
rows.anchor: الأظهر أن موضع السدين في ناحية الشمال

rows.speaker: محمد بن جرير الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reports that an Azerbaijani governor sent an observer through the Khazar region, who described a high wall beyond a deep, strong trench.
rows.anchor: وحكى محمد بن جرير الطبري

rows.speaker: ابن خرداذبة
rows.claim: Ibn Khurdādhbih recounts that al-Wāthiq sent men after a dream; they saw an iron-brick structure bound with molten copper and a locked gate, and al-Bīrūnī inferred a northwestern location.
rows.anchor: في كتاب المسالك والممالك أن الواثق بالله رأى في المنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min dūnihimā means the people were beyond the two barriers, and they scarcely understood speech.
rows.anchor: وجد من دونهما أي من ورائهما مجاوزا عنهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read yafqahūn with passive-like vowels, meaning the people could hardly make others understand; the others read it actively, meaning they knew no other language.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي يفقهون بضم الياء وكسر القاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that Dhū al-Qarnayn understood them is answered either by taking lā yakādūn as a near-negative, so they understood with difficulty, or by supplying that they understood only through laborious gestures and explanation; Razi says the verse supports the first account of kāda.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية تصلح أن يحتج بها على صحة القول الأول في تفسير كاد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view treats Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj as foreign names, as their grammar prevents declension; another derives them from Arabic roots.
rows.anchor: الأول : أنهما إسمان أعجميان موضوعان بدليل منع الصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim reads the names with hamzah, others without it, and one report has Ājūj and Maʾjūj.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم يأجوج ومأجوج بالهمز

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī derives Yaʾjūj from blazing fire and Maʾjūj from the sea's waves, referring to their rapid movement.
rows.anchor: يأجوج مأخوذ من تأجج النار وتلهبها فلسرعتهم في الحركة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another derivation connects Yaʾjūj with the intense saltiness of burning salt and their speed.
rows.anchor: أن يأجوج مأخوذ من تأجج الملح وهو شدة ملوحته

rows.speaker: القتيبي
rows.claim: Al-Qutaybī derives the name from a phrase for an ostrich running rapidly with a rustling sound.
rows.anchor: هو مأخوذ من قولهم أج الظليم في مشيه يئج أجا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl suggests roots meaning a lentil-like seed and the spitting or ejecting of saliva.
rows.anchor: الأج حب كالعدس والمج مج الريق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Their ancestry is variously assigned to the Turks, or Yaʾjūj to the Turks and Maʾjūj to the Jil and Daylam.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا في أنهما من أي الأقوام فقيل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Their reported appearance ranges from extremely short bodies to great height and size, with claws and predatory teeth also attributed to them.
rows.anchor: ثم من الناس من وصفهم بقصر القامة وصغر الجثة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Their corruption is explained as killing people, eating human flesh, or consuming all spring vegetation; Razi leaves the word broad enough for these harms.
rows.anchor: كانوا يقتلون الناس وقيل كانوا يأكلون لحوم الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read kharājan while others read kharjan; some treat the words as synonyms, while others distinguish a contribution from annual state tax.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي خراجا والباقون خرجا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ calls kharāj the original noun and kharj a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء : الخراج هو الاسم الأصلي والخرج كالمصدر

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Quṭrub distinguishes kharj as poll tax and kharāj as land tax.
rows.anchor: وقال قطرب : الخرج الجزية والخراج في الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhū al-Qarnayn declines their payment because God's provision is better than what they offer, echoing Solomon's words.
rows.anchor: كما قال سليمان عليه السلام : { فما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He asks instead for manpower and equipment to build the barrier; another interpretation takes the requested help as project funds rather than personal payment.
rows.anchor: برجال وآلة أبني بها السد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rدم is a barrier more substantial than a simple سد; its root suggests patching a garment's opening with a patch.
rows.anchor: يقال : ردمت الباب أي سددته

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl defines a zubrah of iron as a large piece.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل الزبرة من الحديد القطعة الضخمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All readers lengthen ātūnī except Ḥamzah, who reads iʾtūnī from the verb ‘come’; the omitted preposition bi is understood, as with other verbs used with or without it.
rows.anchor: قراءة الجميع آتوني بمد الألف إلا حمزة فإنه قرأ ائتوني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The iron pieces were stacked until they filled the gap between the mountains; bellows heated them, and molten copper fused them into a solid mass.
rows.anchor: فوضع تلك الزبر بعضها على بعض حتى صارت بحيث تسد ما بين الجبلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction was a striking miracle: God prevented the intense heat from harming the workers who had to blow on the iron.
rows.anchor: فكأنه تعالى صرف تأثير تلك الحرارة العظيمة عن أبدان أولئك النافخين

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf reports that the gap between the two barriers was one hundred farsakhs.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب الكشاف : قيل بعدما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two ṣadaf are the facing sides of the mountains; they are read with two ḍammas or with a ḍamma and sukūn.
rows.anchor: بفتحتين جانبا الجبلين لأنهما يتصادفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qiṭr means molten copper because it drips; the syntax makes it the object of afrigh, with an earlier object omitted for clarity.
rows.anchor: والقطر النحاس المذاب لأنه يقطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tāʾ is dropped from isṭāʿū for ease because it is articulated near ṭāʾ; one reading changes sīn to ṣād.
rows.anchor: فحذف التاء للخفة لأن التاء قريبة المخرج من الطاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They could neither climb the barrier, because it was high and smooth, nor bore through it, because it was hard and thick.
rows.anchor: أن يعلوه أي ما قدروا على الصعود عليه لأجل ارتفاعه وملاسته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This is mercy” may point to the barrier as God's blessing, or to the ability and authority to construct it.
rows.anchor: فقوله هذا إشارة إلى السد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the Day of Judgment approaches, God will flatten the barrier; dakāʾ with long ā means level ground.
rows.anchor: يعني فإذا دنا مجيء القيامة جعل السد دكا أي مدكوكا مسوى بالأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun ‘them’ refers to Gog and Magog; the time of their surging has three readings, with Razi preferring when the barrier is flattened, before the trumpet is blown.
rows.anchor: وكل ذلك محتمل إلا أن الأقرب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One report says they emerge densely from behind the barrier, drink the sea, eat its creatures, vegetation, and people, cannot reach Mecca, Medina, or Jerusalem, then die when animals enter their ears.
rows.anchor: قيل إنهم حين يخرجون من وراء السد يموجون مزدحمين في البلاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Displaying Hell in its terrors to disbelievers is itself a punishment because it fills them with grief.
rows.anchor: فذلك يجري مجرى عقاب الكفار لما يتداخلهم من الغم العظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eyes covered from remembrance means extreme turning away from truth; their inability to hear is worse than ordinary deafness, which can still hear a shout.
rows.anchor: والمراد منه شدة انصرافهم عن قبول الحق

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The Ashʿarī argument takes inability to hear as evidence that capacity accompanies the act: when they did not hear, they lacked the ability.
rows.anchor: على أن الاستطاعة مع الفعل وذلك لأنهم لما لم يسمعوا لم يستطيعوا

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qāḍī reads inability figuratively as aversion and distaste for hearing, like someone saying he cannot bear to look at a person.
rows.anchor: المراد منه نفرتهم عن سماع ذلك الكلام واستثقالهم إياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing disbelievers' rejection of remembrance and the Messenger, the reproachful question asks whether they expect worshipping God's servants to benefit them.
rows.anchor: والمراد أفظنوا أنهم ينتفعون بما عبدوه مع إعراضهم عن تدبر الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Bakr reads with a silent sīn and nominative bāʾ, a reading attributed to ʿAlī: ḥasb is the subject and taking servants as allies is its predicate; other readers use the past-tense form with an omitted notion of benefit.
rows.anchor: بسكون السين ورفع الباء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: God's servants here may mean Jesus and the angels, the devils whom people obey, or idols called servants as in the phrase ‘servants like you.’
rows.anchor: قيل : أراد عيسى والملائكة ، وقيل

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains nuzul as a dwelling or place of lodging; another view takes it as hospitality prepared for a guest.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج إنه المأوى والمنزل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The worst in deeds may be monks; Mujāhid says the People of the Book, and ʿAlī identifies the people of Ḥarūrāʾ when Ibn al-Kawwāʾ asks.
rows.anchor: قيل إنهم هم الرهبان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase generally describes people who think they perform acts of obedience though they are sins, or whose otherwise good works are rejected because of unbelief; they sought reward but were misguided.
rows.anchor: هو الذي يأتي بالأعمال يظنها طاعات وهي في أنفسها معاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of Paradise follows the warning of Hell and encourages faith and righteous action.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر الوعيد أتبعه بالوعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conjoining righteous deeds to faith indicates that good works are distinct from faith.
rows.anchor: عطف عمل الصالحات على الإيمان والمعطوف مغاير للمعطوف عليه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah says Firdaws is the middle and best part of Paradise.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة الفردوس وسط الجنة وأفضلها

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb says no garden is higher than Firdaws, where those commanding right and forbidding wrong dwell.
rows.anchor: وعن كعب ليس في الجنان أعلى من جنة الفردوس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says Firdaws means ‘garden’ in Greek.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد الفردوس هو البستان بالرومية

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report describes one hundred levels of Paradise, with Firdaws the highest, its rivers flowing from it beneath the Throne; believers should ask God for Firdaws.
rows.anchor: وعن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : ( الجنة مائة درجة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some infer that Paradise as a whole is only the believers' lodging, with the further gift of seeing God still to come.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم إنه تعالى جعل الجنة بكليتها نزلا للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection notes that Hell is also called the disbelievers' lodging, apparently leaving no further punishment; Razi answers that being veiled from God is a worse rank, citing 83:15–16, so believers' next gift is vision.
rows.anchor: للكافر بعد حصول جهنم مرتبة أعلى منها وهو كونه محجوبا عن رؤية الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥawlan means moving or changing places; the blessed seek no alternative because Paradise's joys are complete, unlike worldly people who always aspire higher.
rows.anchor: يقال : حال من مكانه حولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After recounting signs and earlier stories, the surah highlights the Qur'an's completeness: if all seas supplied ink to write God's knowledge and wisdom, they would run out before His words.
rows.anchor: لو كتبت كلمات علم الله وحكمه وكان البحر مدادا لها والمراد بالبحر الجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument is that seas are finite whereas God's knowledge is infinite, so finite matter cannot suffice for the infinite.
rows.anchor: البحار كيفما فرضت في الاتساع والعظمة فهي متناهية ومعلومات الله غير متناهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madād is ink for an inkwell or oil for a lamp; Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read yanfad with yāʾ, while others use tāʾ for the feminine subject kalimāt.
rows.anchor: والمداد اسم لما تمد به الدواة من الحبر ولما يمد به السراج من السليط

rows.speaker: حيي بن أخطب
rows.claim: Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab challenges the contrast between wisdom as abundant good and human knowledge as little; the verse answers that God's words remain vastly more abundant.
rows.anchor: وروي أن حيي بن أخطب

rows.speaker: المخالفون
rows.claim: Opponents of the doctrine that God's speech is one argue that the verse's plural ‘words’ establishes multiple divine speech, and that their possible exhaustion disproves their eternality.
rows.anchor: احتج المخالفون على الطعن في قول أصحابنا أن كلام الله تعالى واحد بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī further argues that ‘if We brought its like as ink’ makes God capable of producing an equivalent to His words; a created equivalent would imply the original is created too.
rows.anchor: قال الجبائي : وأيضا قوله

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The Ashʿarī response says the words are expressions for the relations or objects of the eternal attribute of speech.
rows.anchor: أن المراد منه الألفاظ الدالة على تعلقات تلك الصفة الأزلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is instructed to be humble: he shares human qualities with his audience, distinguished only by receiving revelation that God is one.
rows.anchor: أي لا امتياز بيني وبينكم في شيء من الصفات إلا أن الله تعالى أوحى إلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Innamā marks restriction, and God's oneness can be established through scriptural evidence; Razi says he has argued both points elsewhere.
rows.anchor: كلمة { إنما } تفيد الحصر

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The Ashʿarīs interpret hoping to meet the Lord as hoping to see God, while the Muʿtazilites interpret it as meeting God's reward; Razi cites three closing verses as strong evidence for vision.
rows.anchor: وأصحابنا حملوا لقاء الرب على رؤيته والمعتزلة حملوه على لقاء ثواب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hope denotes expectation of benefits reaching one, and fear expectation of harms reaching one.
rows.anchor: والرجاء هو ظن المنافع الواصلة إليه والخوف ظن المضار الواصلة إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A righteous deed must be done for God and free of associating anyone with Him, since otherwise worship may be aimed at ostentation or reputation.
rows.anchor: اعتبر فيه قيدان : أن يؤتى به لله

rows.speaker: جندب بن زهير
rows.claim: Jundub ibn Zuhayr says he does deeds for God but is pleased when someone sees; one Prophetic answer says God rejects work shared with another, applied to deeds intended for display.
rows.anchor: نزلت هذه الآية في جندب بن زهير قال لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A second report promises two rewards, private and public; Razi applies it when a person hopes others will follow the example, distinguishing beginners' sincerity from the perfected person's example.
rows.anchor: وروي أيضا أنه قال له : ( لك أجران أجر السر

none: new surah opening and verse text only
